messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
The “standard deviation” you’re looking for is really the **standard error of the sample mean** under the null hypothesis.  
It’s calculated as:

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]

where  
- \(s = 1.4\) (sample standard deviation)  
- \(n = 40\) (sample size)

\[
SE = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} \approx \frac{1.4}{6.3249} \approx 0.221
\]

So the standard error (i.e., the standard deviation of the null‑hypothesis sampling distribution of the mean) is **about 0.22**.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test. That likely refers to the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis? The standard error of the sample mean is sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they mention "null hypothesis test" maybe they want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the test statistic? For a t-test, the standard error is s / sqrt(n). So compute: 1.4 / sqrt(40). sqrt(40) ≈ 6.3249. 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2213. So standard error ~0.2213.

Alternatively, if they want the standard deviation of the null distribution of the test statistic (t-statistic), that would be sqrt((n-1)/(n-2))? No, that's for t distribution. But likely they want the standard error.

Thus answer: approximately 0.221.

We can also mention that the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test (standard error) is 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 0.221.

Thus answer.
